United Nations specialized agency focusing on agriculture, forestry, and food security.
actors.role: Provides definitions, standards and conducts assessments that shape community‑based forestry policies and practices.

supporting_texts: FAO (1978, p.  1) originally adopted the term "community forestry" as an umbrella term for "any situation which intimately involves local people in a forestry activity".

FAO (2012b) has defined participatory forestry as: "processes and mechanisms which enable people with a direct stake in forest resources to be part of decision-making in all aspects of forest management, including policy formulation processes".

FAO (2010a, pp. 236−237) recorded them as being forests where "communities" are the "holder(s) of management rights of public forests".  FAO (2012b, p. 41) noted that CBF emerged in the Asia and the Pacific region, in part, "in the context of failures by public forestry organizations to effectively protect and manage forests sustainably".  The emergence, growth and evolution of community‑based forestry ... can be traced back to the seminal paper Forestry for local community development (FAO, 1978).
FAO's Forests, Trees and People Programme (FTPP), with its regional hubs, was an important platform for developing and supporting networks to exchange information and share experiences.

significance.supporting_text: FAO’s Forests, Trees and People Programme (FTPP)… was an important platform for developing and supporting networks to exchange information and share experiences.

actors.name: France
actors.description: European nation whose public forests are managed by local government authorities rather than discrete community groups.
actors.role: Serves as an example of a country where communal management rights exist but are administered by state authorities, illustrating limited inclusion of true community‑based forestry regimes.
actors.supporting_text: France and Switzerland remain the only two countries in Europe in which significant areas of the forest estate are managed through some form of communal management rights (FAO, 2010a). However, in both these countries the commune forests are public forests managed by local government authorities and not by discrete community groups.

significance.justification: Illustrates limited presence of communal rights within Europe.
significance.supporting_text: France ... where significant areas ... are managed through some form of communal management rights.

actors.name: World Forestry Congress
actors.description: International forum for forestry professionals and policymakers, convened by the FAO.
actors.role: Provided a platform for the articulation of community‑oriented forest policies, exemplified by the 1978 congress theme “Forests for People,” which helped legitimize community‑based forestry approaches.
actors.supporting_text: In the same year, the eighth World Forestry Congress in Jakarta carried the theme "Forests for People".

significance.justification: Serves as a high‑profile platform that legitimised forest‑people discourse.
significance.supporting_text: the eighth World Forestry Congress in Jakarta carried the theme “Forests for People”.

actors.name: Elinor Ostrom
actors.description: Scholar whose 1990 work popularized the narrative that local communities can autonomously manage forest commons sustainably.
actors.role: Provided the foundational theoretical narrative that underpins community‑based forestry, arguing that granted property rights enable local institutions to regulate and manage natural resources sustainably.
actors.supporting_text: The popularity of community-based forestry as a formal type of forestry rests primarily on a narrative popularized by Ostrom (1990) that local communities, when granted sufficient property rights over local forest commons, can organize autonomously and develop local institutions to regulate the use of natural resources and manage them sustainably.

significance.justification: Her narrative underpins the idea that communities can self‑organize for sustainable forest use.
significance.supporting_text: Narrative popularized by Ostrom (1990) that local communities … can organize autonomously … and manage them sustainably.

actors.name: Tole
actors.description: Researcher who linked community‑based forestry to broader economic and institutional reforms driven by international lenders.
actors.role: Highlighted that CBF initiatives align with IMF and World Bank conditionality lending, which pushes governments to downsize service bureaucracies and adopt decentralized forest management.
actors.supporting_text: Tole (2010, p. 1312) noted that CBF initiatives "fit squarely within the larger economy wide and institutional reforms that many governments have been pursuing under IMF [International Monetary Fund] and World Bank conditionality lending since the 1990s.

significance.justification: Links CBF to IMF/World Bank conditionality and government downsizing of services.
significance.supporting_text: Tole (2010) noted that CBF initiatives “fit squarely within … reforms … under IMF … conditionality lending”.

actors.name: Pokharel
actors.description: Researcher who documented the evolution of community forestry in Nepal.

significance.justification: Shows how community forestry expanded from pure conservation to governance, gender, livelihoods, indicating systemic evolution.

significance.justification: The facility acts as a broker and funder for REDD+‑related carbon projects, opening new financing pathways.
significance.supporting_text: “The facility is designed to act as a broker between buyers and sellers of forest‑related carbon offsets and will also provide funding to countries to build their capacity.”

actors.name: Forest Stewardship Council (FSC)

significance.justification: PEFC was founded to overcome certification barriers for smallholders and community forests.
significance.supporting_text: “PEFC was founded… to overcome some of the difficulties faced by small, family‑owned and community forests.”

concepts.name: Community‑based forestry (CBF)
concepts.definition: A forest management modality in which local communities hold management rights and actively govern the use of forest commons, emerging as a response to the failure of conventional forest industry models and to increasing deforestation in the 1970s‑1980s.
concepts.supporting_text: Functional local management systems were in place to govern how these common forests were used, systems that would currently be considered community-based forestry ... During the 1970s and 1980s, smallholder and community‑based forestry emerged in response partly to a perceived failure of the forest industry development model to lead to socioeconomic development, and partly to the increasing rate of deforestation ... The emergence, growth and evolution of community‑based forestry as a formally recognizable modality of forest management can be traced back to the seminal paper Forestry for local community development (FAO, 1978).
supporting_texts: Functional local management systems were in place to govern how these common forests were used, systems that would currently be considered community-based forestry ... During the 1970s and 1980s, smallholder and community‑based forestry emerged in response partly to a perceived failure of the forest industry development model to lead to socioeconomic development, and partly to the increasing rate of deforestation ... The emergence, growth and evolution of community‑based forestry as a formally recognizable modality of forest management can be traced back to the seminal paper Forestry for local community development (FAO, 1978).

The popularity of community-based forestry as a formal type of forestry rests primarily on a narrative popularized by Ostrom (1990) that local communities, when granted sufficient property rights over local forest commons, can organize autonomously and develop local institutions to regulate the use of natural resources and manage them sustainably.

significance.justification: Frames a systemic approach that reorients forest governance toward local participation and sustainability.
